planting.note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or set out container-grown trees in spring in free-draining soil in full sun, and expect a light first crop within two to three years in a warm climate.

directions: Beldi is the everyday name Moroccan growers give to the traditional, open-pollinated fig populations found in dooryard orchards across the Rif and Middle Atlas foothills, so fruit size and color vary somewhat tree to tree rather than coming from one uniform clone. Most Beldi trees carry a modest breba crop in early summer followed by a heavier main crop in late summer, with medium, thin-skinned fruit that ripens to deep purple-black and is prized for drying as well as fresh eating. Growers typically train the tree as a low, open-centered bush so fruit stays within reach and the canopy sheds summer heat, watering deeply but infrequently once established. In Moroccan kitchens the dried fruit is simmered into tagines with lamb or stuffed with almonds as a winter sweet, extending the harvest well past the short fresh season.
sources: Fig Database — international fig cultivar registry
California Rare Fruit Growers — Fig Fruit Facts

planting.note: Start seed in a shaded nursery bed and transplant three- to four-week-old seedlings into rich, well-drained soil after the last frost, spacing plants to allow repeated cut-and-come-again leaf harvests.

directions: Managu is the Kikuyu and Swahili name for a leafy strain of African nightshade grown across Kenya for its tender, slightly bitter leaves rather than for its small black berries, and it is one of the African indigenous vegetables that Kenyan research stations have worked to preserve and promote for their iron and vitamin content. Seedlings are usually raised in a shaded nursery bed and transplanted into beds or furrows, where the plant branches into a bushy, knee-high clump that tolerates repeated pinching of the growing tips. Leaves are picked young and simmered briefly with onion, tomato, and a touch of milk or butter to soften the bitterness, a preparation traditionally served alongside ugali. Because it reseeds readily and tolerates poor soil, managu is often grown as a low-input kitchen-garden crop alongside other traditional Kenyan greens.
sources: World Vegetable Center — African Indigenous Vegetables
Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) — Traditional Leafy Vegetables

planting.note: Direct-sow after the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed, and provide a trellis, fence, or companion maize stalks since the twining vines climb eagerly once established.

directions: Njahi is the Kikuyu name for a small, dark-seeded lablab bean grown throughout Kenya's central highlands, valued less for its young pods than for the dry black beans harvested once the pods have browned on the vine. Plants form vigorous twining vines that benefit from a trellis, fence, or companion maize stalks to climb, with attractive purple flowers followed by flattened pods that are left on the plant until fully mature and dry. The dried beans are traditionally boiled until tender and mashed with green maize, potatoes, and pumpkin leaves to make mukimo, and njahi is also widely believed in Kenyan households to help nursing mothers produce more milk. Because the vine fixes nitrogen and tolerates dry spells once established, it is often intercropped with maize in smallholder gardens.
sources: Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) — Grain Legumes
World Vegetable Center — Lablab purpureus germplasm notes

planting.note: Direct-sow thickly in warm soil after frost danger has passed, since this landrace is grown primarily for repeated cut-and-come-again leaf harvests rather than for dry pods.

directions: Kunde is the Swahili name used across Kenya and neighboring East African countries for cowpea grown specifically as a leafy green rather than for its pods, with tender young leaves and shoot tips pinched regularly to keep plants bushy and productive. It is one of the most widely eaten African indigenous vegetables, prized for being fast-growing, nutritious, and markedly more drought-tolerant than introduced greens like cabbage. Harvested leaves are chopped and stewed briefly with onion and tomato, often alongside ugali or rice, with a milder flavor than the related bitter green managu. Because the deep-rooted plant fixes its own nitrogen and shrugs off short dry spells, it remains a reliable intercrop in Kenyan smallholder vegetable beds even in poor soils.
sources: World Vegetable Center — African Indigenous Vegetables
Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) — Traditional Leafy Vegetables

planting.note: Direct-sow in flooded or consistently saturated soil once soil temperature is reliably above 70°F, and keep an inch or two of standing water through the vegetative stage since this is a traditional long-season wet-paddy rice.

directions: Phka Rumduol takes its name from the rumduol, Cambodia's fragrant national flower, and is a traditional long-grain jasmine-type rice grown in the rain-fed lowland paddies of provinces such as Battambang and Takeo. The variety is photoperiod-sensitive and matures late in the wet season, producing slender, aromatic grains that cook up soft and fragrant, qualities that helped it earn international best-rice recognition at rice-trade competitions in the early 2010s under the export name Malys Angkor. Farmers traditionally raise seedlings in a flooded nursery bed and transplant them by hand into puddled paddy soil, maintaining shallow standing water through most of the growing season before draining the field ahead of harvest. Because of its long maturity window, it is grown as a single wet-season crop rather than the multiple short-cycle crops used for high-yield modern varieties.
sources: The Rice Trader — World's Best Rice awards records
Cambodian Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries — rice variety documentation
